intro_md:
Fifty-two machine-learning research questions, each asking a model to propose a better scientific method than the published ones.

ML-Relay follows the design of MLS-Bench. Where ML engineering combines many techniques to push a metric on one dataset, ML science makes one atomic, generalisable contribution — a better loss, criterion, schedule, solver, search policy or architectural block — that transfers across models, data and tasks. Each task here isolates such a component inside a fixed, already-built research pipeline: the model edits one file within one line range, and everything else — data, training loop, evaluation — runs as it is. The published reference methods for the question are ported to the same pipeline and measured on it; they are anchors, not the assignment. A submission is scored by where it lands relative to the reference methods, per evaluation setting: the weakest reference anchors 0 and the **strongest reference anchors 10%** of the scale, so 90% of the range is headroom above the state of the field. The task score is the geometric mean across several genuinely different settings, so a component has to generalise to score well. Running every baseline inside the pipeline and checking that their order matches the literature is how each task earned its place: it proves the editable component is the one that matters and that a better method, once written, will be measured.

**Composition.** 36 of the 50 tasks are newly constructed for ML-Relay. The other 14 are drawn from MLS-Bench, selected for quality. MLS-Bench Lite, by contrast, consisted mainly of evaluation scaffolding; every task here poses a research question with measured anchors.

**What ships.** Fifty-two self-contained Harbor tasks under `tasks/`. Each holds `instruction.md` (the question, the editable file and range, the interface, the reference methods with citations, the metrics), `environment/` (a Dockerfile that builds the pipeline and fetches the task's data from public origins, plus the agent-start workspace), `tests/` (the evaluation, mounted only at verification) and `solution/` (an oracle that replays one reference method). Run a task with `harbor run -p tasks/<task>`.

tasks.question: A flow-based VLA plans an action chunk from an observation that is already d steps stale when the chunk arrives; with the policy and the delay fixed, design the rule at the chunk boundary — what to freeze, what to inpaint, how to blend — so execution stays smooth and success survives the delay.

baselines.name: naive asynchronous chunk switch, SmolVLA default (Shukor et al., 2025; unmodified starter)
temporal ensembling, ACT (Zhao et al., 2023; lerobot ACTTemporalEnsembler)
IT-RTC soft-mask inpainting as lerobot's RTCProcessor runs it (Black et al., 2025; arXiv:2605.08168 protocol)
hard-mask inpainting, RTC's own ablation (Black et al., 2025)
real-time chunking, the paper's Kinetix reference with full VJP guidance (Black et al., 2025)
fresh chunk executed from step 0, replaying the elapsed actions (null)

tasks.title: Teaching a Chunked Flow Policy From Success Alone
tasks.question: With the imitation-trained SmolVLA, the online rollout budget in the simulator and a binary success reward fixed, design the policy-gradient objective over action chunks — how the advantage is estimated and assigned at chunk or trajectory level, and what likelihood surrogate the flow-matching expert gets — so that task success rises most reliably above the imitation policy.

baselines.name: the imitation policy unchanged, no RL (null; the SFT row of the papers)
RIPT-VLA: leave-one-out advantages over K rollouts of one initial state, PPO clipping, rejection of uninformative groups (Tan et al., 2025)
SimpleVLA-RL: group-relative advantages with clip-higher and no KL (Li et al., 2025)
πRL Flow-SDE: ODE-to-SDE likelihood for the flow expert, PPO with a learned value (Chen et al., 2025; Flow-GRPO, Liu et al., 2025)

tasks.title: Keeping LLM RL Stable When the Sampler Is Not the Trainer
tasks.question: With the model, data, reward, RL loop and an imposed sampler–trainer mismatch fixed, design the per-token correction to the policy-gradient objective — from the trainer's and the sampler's log-probs, the sampler's top-K log-probs and the advantage — so that training stays stable and reward keeps rising as the mismatch grows.
